metadata.title: Poland Energy Sector Attacks – 29 December 2025
metadata.description: Interactive, defensive reconstruction of the coordinated destructive cyberattacks against the Polish energy sector on 29 December 2025, based solely on two public CERT Polska reports. All facts, dates, technologies and attack paths are drawn from the source reports; nothing has been invented.

sources.title: Follow-Up Analysis of the 29 December 2025 Energy Sector Incident

metadata.location_accuracy_notice: Exact facility locations are not publicly specified in the source reports. Visual positions in this application are schematic and do not represent real coordinates or sites.
metadata.attribution_notice: CERT Polska links the direct attack infrastructure to the activity cluster publicly known as 'Static Tundra' / 'Berserk Bear' / 'Ghost Blizzard' / 'Dragonfly'. Similarities between the wipers and 'Sandworm' tooling were found too weak to be conclusive. Attribution is presented here exactly as the reports frame it, not as settled fact.
metadata.page_notice: Page numbers are PDF page numbers as shown by a PDF viewer. The number printed in each report's footer is one lower.

incidents.name: Renewable Energy Facilities (wind & solar farms)
incidents.facility_type: At least 30 wind and solar farms (Grid Connection Point substations)
incidents.summary: At least 30 wind and solar farms were attacked. The attack caused loss of communication between the facilities and distribution system operators (DSOs) and loss of remote control, but did not affect ongoing electricity generation and did not impact the stability of the Polish power system. Destructive actions targeted OT devices at the Grid Connection Point (GCP) substations and appeared at least partially automated.
initial_access: Internet-exposed FortiGate VPN interface without multi-factor authentication
Accounts statically defined in the FortiGate configuration
Likely credential reuse across multiple facilities
Some FortiGate devices had been vulnerable in the past, including to remote code execution
actions: Logged into Hitachi RTU560 web interface with default 'Default' account and uploaded corrupted firmware (240 bytes of 0xFF at the program entry point), causing a reboot loop
Deleted all files on Mikronika RTUs over SSH as root using default credentials
Deleted essential system files on Hitachi Relion 650 relays via default FTP account

Accessed Mikronika Syndis HMI via RDP using known default local admin password; enabled admin shares and SMB (TCP 445) via PowerShell, then ran Impacket reconnaissance and executed DynoWiper (C:\Source.exe)
Factory-reset all Moxa NPort devices, changed passwords and set IP addresses to unreachable values (e.g. 127.0.0.1)
Factory-reset all analyzed FortiGate devices to hinder recovery and erase traces
impact: Loss of communication between facilities and the DSO
Loss of remote control / loss of view
No impact on Polish power system stability

incidents.name: Large CHP Plant
incidents.facility_type: Combined heat and power plant supplying heat to nearly half a million customers
incidents.summary: A large CHP plant was targeted after a long-term infiltration of its IT infrastructure, with theft of sensitive information and compromise of privileged Active Directory accounts. DynoWiper was distributed via Group Policy, but the organization's EDR blocked runtime execution on more than 100 machines using a canary mechanism. The attacker also attempted to destroy data directly on server disks and RAID arrays.
initial_access: FortiGate SSL-VPN portal with statically defined accounts and no two-factor authentication
Connections via Tor nodes and compromised Polish and foreign IP addresses
actions: Used SSL-VPN bookmarks with statically configured credentials to reach jump hosts via RDP
Reconnaissance with nircmd (screenshots), PsExec, nslookup, ping, Advanced Port/IP Scanner, focused on SCADA/OT systems
Deployed rsocx reverse SOCKS proxy (r.exe / rsocx.exe) to a server at 31.172.71[.]5
LSASS memory dump; Rubeus Diamond Ticket; ntds.dit, SAM and SYSTEM hive theft via reg and vssadmin
Exfiltrated compressed data over HTTP to 31.172.71[.]5 via Invoke-RestMethod
Stole FortiGate configuration files via Microsoft Edge in private mode
Added a permissive FortiGate firewall rule with logging disabled, mimicking an existing institution name
Distributed DynoWiper via a Group Policy Object pointing to a network share
Attempted direct server-disk destruction using Tiny Core Linux booted over KVM with dd, and attempted RAID array reconfiguration via Intel Rapid Storage Technology
impact: DynoWiper execution BLOCKED by EDR canary mechanism on 100+ machines
A second, slightly modified wiper attempt also unsuccessful
Long-term theft of sensitive operational data and credentials
Attempted but uncertain destruction of server disks / RAID arrays

source_references.section: Attack on the Large CHP Plant
Destruction of Data on Server Disks

incidents.name: Second (smaller) CHP Plant
incidents.facility_type: CHP plant supplying heat to approximately 50,000 residents
incidents.summary: A smaller CHP plant's industrial control systems were attacked at around 7:00 a.m. The attacker reached the plant's OT network through a novel path: a compromised wind-farm FortiGate, a Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router, an SSH tunnel into a DSO-managed private APN, and a WAGO PFC200 controller bridging the APN to the plant's OT network. Siemens PLCs were placed in STOP mode, shutting down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment system. CERT Polska states this is, to its knowledge, the first observed real-world use of a private APN as an OT access vector.
initial_access: Compromised FortiGate VPN/firewall at a wind farm (shared with the renewable-energy incident)
SSH access to a Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router (how the changed password was obtained is unknown)
SSH tunnel into the DSO-managed private APN
WAGO PFC200 web admin interface reachable on its WAN interface with default 'admin' credentials
affected_assets: WAGO PFC200 PLC with integrated cellular modem
Siemens S7-300, S7-1200 and S7-1500 PLCs
7 Moxa serial device servers and 3 Moxa network switches
ABB ACS series variable frequency drives
Schneider Electric ATV6xx variable frequency drives
actions: Logged into the Teltonika RUTX50 via SSH multiple times during December 2025 and established an SSH tunnel to the private APN
Scanned the private APN for VNC, HTTP, S7 and Modbus services (from 18 December 2025)
Used default credentials on the WAGO PFC200 web interface; SSH likely enabled via the web interface, then tunneled into the plant's OT network
Unsuccessful login attempts against the plant's firewall/VPN web interface (admin, user, and a deployer username)
Scanned the internal network (S7 102/TCP, Modbus 502/TCP, CODESYS 11740/TCP, RTSP 554/TCP, RDP, VNC, HTTP/HTTPS)
Connected to three Siemens PLCs over S7 on 25 December; on 29 December placed S7-300, S7-1200 and S7-1500 PLCs in STOP mode, password-protected against changes
Factory-reset 7 Moxa serial device servers and 3 Moxa switches, changed passwords, set IPs to unreachable values (automated)
Connected to two ABB ACS drive web interfaces (actions unknown); failed to reach Schneider Electric ATV6xx drives (wrong port)
Corrupted the WAGO controller's partition table; factory-reset the Teltonika and the wind-farm FortiGate to cover tracks
impact: Interruption of the cogeneration process (short-term outage only)
No disruption to heat or electricity supply for customers
WAGO controller, Teltonika router and FortiGate rendered inoperable / factory-reset (track covering)

incidents.name: Manufacturing Sector Company
incidents.facility_type: Private manufacturing company (opportunistic target, not an energy entity)
incidents.summary: On the same day, and in coordination with the energy-sector attacks, the attacker targeted a manufacturing company via a previously vulnerable Fortinet device whose configuration had been stolen and publicly leaked. Persistence was established through FortiGate's built-in scripting, and the LazyWiper PowerShell wiper was distributed via Group Policy. CERT Polska describes the target as opportunistic and not linked to the other affected organizations.
initial_access: Fortinet perimeter device, previously vulnerable, with a stolen and publicly disclosed configuration (posted on a criminal forum)
Later, SSL-VPN tunnel using previously obtained credentials
actions: Created two weekly FortiGate CLI scripts to exfiltrate a privileged user's password and to weaken security settings (unset two-factor, unset trusthost)
Exfiltrated script output to an attacker-controlled Slack channel via FortiGate's Slack notification feature
Used Impacket for lateral movement
Gained administrative access to a domain controller and distributed the LazyWiper PowerShell wiper via a Group Policy Object pulling from a network share
impact: Deployment of the LazyWiper destructive PowerShell wiper
Persistent FortiGate access surviving password changes
Credential exfiltration to an attacker-controlled Slack channel

source_references.section: Attack on a Manufacturing Sector Company

timeline.title: Early infiltration of the large CHP plant
timeline.description: Suspicious activity in the large CHP plant's infrastructure: reconnaissance, unauthorized data access and attempts to obtain credentials. First attacker activity dated to March–May 2025; access gained to a jump host via a FortiGate interface address, then to the domain controller.

source_references.section: Early Activity in the Organization's Infrastructure

timeline.title: Privilege escalation and ntds.dit theft (first cluster)
timeline.description: Base64 ZIP decoded via certutil, LSASS dump, Rubeus Diamond Ticket, and a dump of the full Active Directory database (ntds.dit) in the second half of July. The first activity cluster then went quiet.

timeline.title: November 2025 VPN logins (network indicators)
timeline.description: VPN logins recorded from several IP addresses used against multiple entities (per the Indicators of Compromise), including 193.200.17[.]163, 185.82.127[.]20, 41.111.178[.]225 and 159.69.50[.]242.

timeline.title: HMI configuration changes at a renewable facility
timeline.description: On a Mikronika Syndis HMI (Windows 10), the attacker enabled administrative shares and created a firewall rule 'Microsoft Update' allowing TCP 445, enabling SMB disk access and remote command execution, all via PowerShell.

timeline.title: SSH access to Teltonika router & private APN scanning begins
timeline.description: Recovered logs show successful SSH logins to the Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router. From 18 December the attacker repeatedly scanned the private APN for VNC, HTTP, S7 and Modbus services, and discovered the WAGO PFC200 controller.

source_references.section: Activity at the Wind Farm / Leveraging the Private APN

timeline.title: Reconnaissance of the second CHP plant OT network
timeline.description: After gaining access to the CHP plant's network, the attacker conducted reconnaissance and attempts to expand access between 18 and 25 December 2025, including unsuccessful firewall login attempts.

source_references.section: Reconnaissance of the CHP Plant Network

timeline.title: Internal network scan of the second CHP plant
timeline.description: Internal network scanning targeting S7 (102/TCP), Modbus (502/TCP), CODESYS (11740/TCP), RTSP (554/TCP), RDP, VNC and HTTP/HTTPS. In one subnet, scanning began at the SCADA system's IP, suggesting prior target identification.

timeline.title: Further reconnaissance (RDP hosts) at the second CHP plant
timeline.description: Connections to remote-desktop ports on two hosts, most likely manual attempts to identify valid credentials; no successful connection was found.

timeline.title: ping / nslookup reconnaissance on a domain controller
timeline.description: Domain controller event log shows nslookup and ping process creations (including names containing 'scada' and 'fortigate') on 22 December 2025.

timeline.title: S7 connections to three Siemens PLCs
timeline.description: The attacker successfully established S7 connections to three Siemens PLCs, most likely reconnaissance in preparation for subsequent destructive actions.

timeline.title: Network scanning and login attempts on Mikronika RTUs
timeline.description: Recovered Mikronika device logs indicate that on 25 December 2025, at all facilities where the device was deployed, the attacker conducted network scanning and login attempts.

timeline.title: DynoWiper variant A compiled
timeline.description: DynoWiper samples Source.exe and dynacom_update.exe carry a compilation timestamp of 2025-12-26 13:51:11 UTC (version A). Compilation dates can be forged but match the attack chronology.

timeline.title: Disruptive actions at the second CHP plant
timeline.description: Attacker activity in the CHP plant network ran from ~05:30 to ~10:10 a.m. Siemens S7-300/1200/1500 PLCs were placed in STOP mode (password-protected), shutting down the steam turbine and process-water treatment and interrupting cogeneration. Moxa devices were factory-reset. Recovery began ~07:30 a.m. while the attacker was still present.

source_references.section: Disruptive Actions at the CHP Plant

timeline.title: Destructive actions at renewable facilities
timeline.description: Destructive actions initiated at each affected facility against accessible devices. RTU event log shows firmware 13.5.3.0 transferred at 13:57 on 2025-12-29, followed by a manual reset and gateway restart. Devices damaged in ascending IP order; the activity appeared at least partially automated.

timeline.title: DynoWiper distributed via GPO at the large CHP plant – blocked by EDR
timeline.description: DynoWiper was placed on a network share and executed via a Group Policy Object. The EDR blocked runtime execution using a canary mechanism, halting data overwriting on 100+ machines. A second, slightly modified attempt (schtask.exe variants compiled 2025-12-29) also failed.

timeline.title: LazyWiper distributed via GPO at the manufacturing company
timeline.description: Coordinated with the energy-sector attacks, the attacker used a domain controller to distribute the LazyWiper PowerShell wiper via a Group Policy Object pulling the payload from a network share.
